newsitem.title: USA: U.S. economists project interest rate hike by May.
newsitem.headline: U.S. economists project interest rate hike by May.

text.p: U.S. economists expect the Federal Reserve to keep interest rates unchanged at its March 25 policy meeting despite recent hawkish comments by Fed chief Alan Greenspan, a Reuters survey showed Thursday.

But the odds of a rate hike in May appear higher, according to the survey of 35 economists at U.S. primary dealers, the banks that buy Treasury debt at auctions and are responsible for distributing them to investors.
Twenty-four of those surveyed said the Fed would not hike rates in March, but many said they could change their minds as new economic data become available.
Five economists forecast a rate hike at the March 25 Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting, while another six put the chance of a credit tightening at 50-50.
The survey, conducted Thursday, included 35 of the nation's 37 primary dealers.
The last time the Fed changed rates was in January, 1996, when it lowered the federal funds rate by 25 basis points.
The Fed controls the Fed funds rate, which is the interest rate charged for overnight, interbank loans, and the discount rate, which is the rate charged by the Fed for loans to banks.

Greenspan's remarks Wednesday before the Senate Banking Committee "raised the odds somewhat, but the odds still remain less than 50 percent," said Anthony Karydakis, senior financial economist at First Chicago Capital Markets Inc., adding that the Fed will more likely raise rates at its subsequent meeting on May 20.
"He reminded people how close they (FOMC members) are to beginning the tightening process," Karydakis said.

Greenspan said that while prospects in the economy are "favorable," risks of future inflation pressures -- particularly wages -- have increased, and warned the Fed won't be afraid to make a pre-emptive strike to keep inflation at bay. His remarks echoed what he and other Fed officials have been saying since last summer.
Still, most economists said it is too early to make a definitive call for a meeting a month away, noting the Fed still needs to see economic data for February.
"A week from now, the odds (of a rate hike) will be closer to 80 percent or closer to 30 percent," said David Resler, chief economist at Nomura Securities International Inc.

Should the Fed remain on the sidelines in March, a May rate hike looks more likely, economists said. The Reuters poll found that 25 economists forecast a rate hike at or before the May FOMC meeting, while two more expected the first rate increase sometime in the second half of the year.

The results differed somewhat from a poll taken after the February 4-5 FOMC meeting. At that time only 16 of 31 economists polled predicted a rate hike by May. The other 15 figured the Fed would tighten in the second half of the year or not at all in 1997.

In the current survey, six economists did not project a move in 1997, while one called for a rate cut this year. Further, 24 of the 35 economists forecast a federal funds rate above 5.50 percent by year end, with 20 of those predicting 5.75 percent or higher.
The fed funds rate currently stands at 5.25 percent and the discount rate is at 5 percent.

Changes by the Fed in the interest rate it controls influences other interest rates, such as the prime lending rates that banks charge business, which in turn influence interest rates charged for everything from credit cards to home mortgage loans.
